gold_output.title: What is RAG?
gold_output.script: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, combines a language generator with an external collection of documents. The paper argues that pretrained language models can store a lot of factual knowledge, but they can be difficult to update, difficult to inspect, and can produce hallucinations. RAG adds a non-parametric memory that can be searched for relevant information. In the paper, that memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia, and a neural retriever based on Dense Passage Retrieval selects relevant passages. A BART sequence-to-sequence generator then uses the input together with the retrieved passage to produce the output. The authors study two variants. RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved document for the whole output, while RAG-Token can use different documents for different output tokens. Across knowledge-intensive tasks, the authors report strong results, including state-of-the-art results on three open-domain question-answering tasks. They also report that RAG generates more specific, diverse, and factual language than a parametric-only BART baseline. A key practical advantage is that the external index can be replaced to update the model's accessible knowledge without retraining the generator.

gold_output.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
gold_output.script:
The paper introduces Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, as a general-purpose way to combine pretrained parametric memory with an explicit non-parametric memory. The motivation is that pretrained language models can store substantial factual knowledge, but their knowledge is difficult to revise or inspect, and they may hallucinate. Earlier retrieval-augmented approaches such as REALM and ORQA had explored differentiable retrieval but were focused on extractive open-domain question answering. RAG brings retrieval into sequence-to-sequence generation.

The architecture has two main components. First is the retriever p_eta(z|x), implemented using Dense Passage Retrieval. DPR uses a BERT-based query encoder and a BERT-based document encoder. The dense representations are compared using maximum inner product search to obtain the top-k documents. Second is the generator p_theta(y_i|x,z,y_1:i-1), implemented with BART-large. The original input and retrieved passage are concatenated and supplied to BART. The retrieved document is treated as a latent variable, so the model marginalizes over the top retrieved documents rather than selecting one document as a permanently correct answer.

The paper proposes two formulations. RAG-Sequence assumes that one retrieved document is responsible for the complete generated sequence. Its probability is approximated by summing the generator probability over the top-k retrieved documents, weighted by the retriever probability. RAG-Token instead allows a different latent document for each output token. This gives the model the ability to combine information from multiple retrieved documents. The authors jointly train the retriever and generator from input-output pairs without direct supervision over which document should be retrieved. They optimize the negative marginal log-likelihood, keep the document encoder and index fixed, and fine-tune the query encoder and BART generator.

For experiments, the authors use a December 2018 Wikipedia dump. Articles are divided into disjoint 100-word chunks, producing 21 million documents. They build a FAISS maximum-inner-product index and retrieve documents for each query. The evaluation covers open-domain QA, abstractive QA on MS-MARCO, Jeopardy question generation, and FEVER fact verification.

On open-domain QA, RAG-Sequence reaches 44.5 Exact Match on Natural Questions, 45.2 on WebQuestions, and 52.2 on CuratedTrec; RAG-Token reaches 44.1, 45.5, and 50.0 respectively. For TriviaQA, the reported scores depend on the test setup: RAG-Sequence obtains 56.8 on the standard test and 68.0 on the TQA-Wiki setup. The authors report state-of-the-art results on the four open-domain QA tasks considered, with the qualification that the TQA claim is for the T5-comparable split.

For MS-MARCO generation, RAG-Sequence obtains a BLEU-1 score of 44.2 compared with 41.6 for BART. The paper reports that RAG generations hallucinate less and are factually correct more often than BART. For Jeopardy question generation, RAG-Token has a Q-BLEU-1 score of 22.2, compared with 19.7 for BART. Human evaluators preferred RAG over BART on factuality in 42.7% of cases versus 7.1% for BART, and also found RAG more specific in the pairwise evaluation.

The paper also studies retrieval ablations. Learned retrieval improves results over a frozen retriever across the reported tasks. BM25 performs best on FEVER, which the authors suggest may be because FEVER claims are heavily entity-centric and therefore well suited to word-overlap retrieval. The authors also demonstrate index hot-swapping: replacing a 2016 Wikipedia index with a 2018 index changes the knowledge available to RAG without retraining. Overall, the paper's central result is that retrieval gives a sequence-to-sequence generator explicit access to external text while preserving the flexibility of generation.

gold_output.post:
One of the key ideas behind Retrieval-Augmented Generation is surprisingly simple: don't force a generator to keep all useful knowledge inside its parameters.

Lewis et al.'s RAG paper combines a pretrained sequence-to-sequence generator with a non-parametric memory. In their experiments, the memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia, retrieved with Dense Passage Retrieval, while BART provides the generation model.

The paper studies two variants. RAG-Sequence uses one retrieved document for the whole sequence; RAG-Token can use different documents for different generated tokens. On the reported tasks, RAG achieves strong results, including 44.5 Exact Match on Natural Questions for RAG-Sequence and 44.2 BLEU-1 on MS-MARCO versus 41.6 for BART.

The most practical result is the index hot-swap experiment: changing the external Wikipedia index changes the knowledge available to the model without retraining the generator.

The broader lesson from this paper is that retrieval and generation can play different roles: retrieval provides access to external text, while the generator turns that information into flexible output.

request.task: Explain the RAG-Sequence probability formulation and why the document is treated as a latent variable.

gold_output.answer: RAG treats the retrieved document z as a latent variable. For RAG-Sequence, the top-k retrieved documents are considered, and the sequence probability is approximated by summing the generator probability for the complete output under each retrieved document, weighted by the retriever probability. In other words, the model does not commit to one retrieved passage as the only explanation for the output; it marginalizes over the retrieved candidates. The paper contrasts this with RAG-Token, where the latent document can change for each output token.

gold_output.title: Study explores combining retrieval with language generation
gold_output.body:
Researchers introduce Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), a framework that combines a pretrained language generator with an external collection of documents. The work addresses limitations the authors identify in parametric language models, including difficulty revising stored knowledge, limited ability to inspect accessed knowledge, and hallucinations.

In the study, a Dense Passage Retriever searches a dense vector index of Wikipedia for relevant passages. A BART sequence-to-sequence generator then uses the input and retrieved text to produce an output. The researchers compare two formulations: RAG-Sequence, which uses the same retrieved document for the full output, and RAG-Token, which can use different documents for different generated tokens.

The experiments cover open-domain question answering, abstractive question answering, Jeopardy question generation, and fact verification. RAG-Sequence reaches 44.5 Exact Match on Natural Questions and 44.2 BLEU-1 on MS-MARCO, compared with 41.6 for the BART baseline on the latter task. Human evaluations for Jeopardy question generation also favor RAG on reported factuality and specificity comparisons.

The study additionally demonstrates that replacing the external index can change the knowledge available to the system without retraining the generator.
